name: Vladimir Lenin
info: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, known as Lenin, was a Russian Marxist revolutionary who led the Bolsheviks in the October Revolution of 1917 and headed the Soviet government until his death in 1924.

facts.born: 22 April 1870 (10 April Old Style) in Simbirsk, now Ulyanovsk, Russian Empire, the third of eight children of Ilya Nikolayevich Ulyanov, a school director, and Maria Alexandrovna Ulyanova (née Blank)
facts.died: 21 January 1924 at Gorki, aged 53, after a coma; the official cause was recorded as an incurable disease of the blood vessels
facts.role: Leader of the Bolshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party from 1903; Chairman of the Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom) of Soviet Russia from 1917 and of the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1924
facts.known: leading the Bolsheviks in the October Revolution of 1917; the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk; the Red Terror and the Cheka; victory in the Russian Civil War; the Communist International; the New Economic Policy; the formation of the Soviet Union; Leninism and the theory of the vanguard party

t: Moved to revolutionary politics by his brother's execution in 1887, Lenin became a Marxist theorist, led the Bolshevik faction from 1903 and headed the government that took power in Petrograd in October 1917.

His government redistributed land, nationalised banks and large industry, left the First World War at a heavy cost in territory, won the Russian Civil War, and by 1918 had made Russia a one-party state in which the Cheka carried out the Red Terror.

Supporters see a champion of revolutionary socialism and internationalism; critics accuse him of founding a totalitarian dictatorship responsible for mass killings and repression, and historians still disagree on how far Stalin continued his work.
dyk: In 1917 the German government allowed 32 Russian citizens, Lenin among them, to travel through its territory to Russia; the train was said to be sealed, but it was not truly sealed, and the passengers were allowed to get off, for example to spend a night in Frankfurt.
ev: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov is born in Simbirsk
His brother Aleksandr is executed; Lenin enters Kazan University and is expelled after a student demonstration
At the second Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in London the party splits into Lenin's Bolsheviks and Martov's Mensheviks
Lenin returns to Russia in April and in October the Bolsheviks overthrow the Provisional Government; he becomes head of the new Council of People's Commissars
Russia signs the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the Red Terror begins, and Lenin is shot and severely wounded by Fanny Kaplan
Lenin introduces the New Economic Policy and bans factions within the party
The Soviet Union is formed; Lenin has his first stroke in May
Lenin dies at Gorki and is laid in a mausoleum on Red Square

sections.early:
Lenin was born Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov in Simbirsk, now Ulyanovsk, on 22 April 1870, the third of eight children. His father, Ilya Nikolayevich Ulyanov, came from a family of former serfs and rose to be Director of Public Schools for the province, a post that gave him hereditary noble status; he oversaw the foundation of over 450 schools. His mother, Maria Alexandrovna, née Blank, was the well-educated daughter of a physician and largely indifferent to Christianity. His parents were monarchists and liberal conservatives, committed to the emancipation reform of 1861, and Lenin excelled at the Simbirsk Classical Gymnasium.

In January 1886 his father died of a brain haemorrhage, and Lenin, then 15, renounced his belief in God. In May 1887 his elder brother Aleksandr, who had joined a revolutionary cell bent on assassinating Tsar Alexander III, was executed. Lenin nevertheless graduated at the top of his class with a gold medal and entered Kazan University in August 1887 to study law. He took part in a December demonstration against restrictions on student societies, was arrested and expelled, and was exiled to the family's Kokushkino estate, where he read Chernyshevsky's What Is to Be Done? In Samara from 1889 he translated the Communist Manifesto and read Plekhanov, and in 1890 he took his law examinations externally at the University of St Petersburg, gaining the equivalent of a first-class degree with honours.
sections.rise:
Lenin moved to Saint Petersburg in late 1893 and rose to a senior position in a Marxist cell. He was arrested with about 40 activists and charged with sedition, spent a year in prison, and in February 1897 was sentenced without trial to three years' exile in Siberia, at Shushenskoye, where Nadezhda Krupskaya joined him and they married on 10 July 1898. In 1900 he left Russia for Western Europe to help launch the newspaper Iskra. He first used the pseudonym Lenin in December 1901, and in 1902 published What Is to Be Done?, setting out the need for a vanguard party. At the second Congress of the party in London in July 1903 Lenin's supporters won a majority on the question of strong party leadership; he called them Bolsheviks, and Martov's followers became the Mensheviks, who accused Lenin of being a despot and autocrat.

During the Revolution of 1905 Lenin urged violent insurrection and endorsed robbing post offices, trains and banks to fund the party; the best known robbery, of the State Bank in Tiflis in June 1907, was led by Joseph Stalin. During the First World War he urged socialists to turn the war into a continent-wide civil war. After the February Revolution of 1917 he returned through Germany, reached Petrograd in April and set out his April Theses against the Provisional Government. After the July Days he was accused of being a German agent and hid. On 10 October the Central Committee voted ten to two for an armed insurrection, against the objections of Zinoviev and Kamenev, and the Provisional Government was overthrown that month. Lenin proposed Trotsky as head of the new government but accepted the chairmanship himself.
sections.deeds:
The new government's first decrees nationalised the landed estates of the aristocracy and the Orthodox Church for redistribution to the peasants, set an eight-hour working day, guaranteed free secular education and nationalised the banks. Lenin urged peace with Germany and, after the Central Powers resumed their advance in February 1918, persuaded a small majority of the Central Committee to accept the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March. It transferred to German control 26% of the former Empire's population and three-quarters of its coal and iron deposits. The Constituent Assembly elected in November 1917, in which the Bolsheviks won about a quarter of the vote, was forcibly disbanded in January 1918. The Left Socialist-Revolutionaries left the government in March 1918, and by 1918 and 1919 other socialists had been expelled from the soviets, so that Russia had become a one-party state.

The Red Army, which Trotsky organised, defeated the White armies in the Russian Civil War, and the Soviet government also fought the Polish–Soviet War, in which the Red Army was defeated at Warsaw and the Peace of Riga was signed in March 1921. In March 1919 Lenin helped found the Communist International. Facing famine, strikes and uprisings, in 1921 he introduced the New Economic Policy, which allowed peasants to sell produce on the open market and permitted small private industry, while basic industry, transport and foreign trade stayed under state control. He called it "state capitalism", and many Bolsheviks thought it a betrayal of socialist principles. On 30 December 1922 the Congress of Soviets ratified the formation of the Soviet Union, a plan Lenin had pressed against Stalin's proposal to absorb the republics into the Russian state.
sections.opponents:
Lenin repeatedly stressed the need for terror and violence, and in December 1917 ordered the founding of the Cheka. In August 1918 he telegraphed the Bolsheviks of Penza to suppress a peasant insurrection by publicly hanging at least 100 "known kulaks, rich men, [and] bloodsuckers". The Red Terror was begun by a decree of September 1918; no records survive to give a figure for its dead, and historians' estimates range from 10,000 to 15,000 and from 50,000 to 140,000. Lenin never witnessed the killings and publicly distanced himself from them, but he regularly called for executions in coded telegrams and confidential notes. Concentration camps were set up from 1919, holding about 70,000 prisoners by October 1923, and their inmates were used as slave labour. In May 1922 he issued a decree calling for the execution of anti-Bolshevik priests, causing between 14,000 and 20,000 deaths. The famine of 1921 killed around five million people, and requisitioning and grain exports were said to have worsened it. The Kronstadt rebellion of March 1921 was crushed with thousands of deaths.

Opposition came from the left as well. Left Communists and the Workers' Opposition criticised the decline of democratic institutions, Karl Kautsky and Rosa Luxemburg condemned the regime's anti-democratic nature, and Peter Kropotkin called the seizure of power "the burial of the Russian Revolution". Biographers such as Robert Service describe a man intolerant of opposition, for whom the end always justified the means.
sections.last:
Lenin's health suffered after Fanny Kaplan shot him on 30 August 1918; she was captured at once and executed on 3 September. By the second half of 1921 he had hyperacusis, insomnia and regular headaches. In April 1922 surgeons removed bullets from the 1918 attempt, but the symptoms continued, and his doctors were unsure of the cause. He had his first stroke in May 1922, a second in December and a third in March 1923, which took away his speech. From December 1922 to January 1923 he dictated what became known as Lenin's Testament, recommending that Stalin be removed as General Secretary and criticising Trotsky's self-assurance. In the Georgian affair he saw Stalin's proposal to fold the Soviet republics into the Russian state as Great Russian ethnic chauvinism, and he grew increasingly critical of Stalin, who from December 1922 controlled who had access to him.

On 21 January 1924 Lenin fell into a coma and died at the age of 53. Around a million mourners viewed the body over three days at the House of Trade Unions, and his funeral on 27 January ended with his body being placed in a mausoleum on Red Square. Trotsky was absent and later claimed that Stalin had sent him the wrong date. Against Krupskaya's protests, the body was embalmed for long-term public display, and in 1925 an institute was set up to dissect the brain, which showed severe sclerosis. Stalin succeeded him as the pre-eminent figure in the Soviet government.
sections.legacy:
Lenin's administration laid the framework for the system of government that ruled Russia for seven decades and provided the model for later Communist-led states. After his death Stalin's administration established Marxism–Leninism, and states claiming to follow Lenin's ideas formed variants such as Maoism and Castroism, though many Western communists later thought his ideas irrelevant to their goals. In the Soviet Union a cult of personality grew up around him, which Krupskaya criticised and Lenin had not wanted; Petrograd was renamed Leningrad in 1924, and his writings were treated like scripture and edited, with those unhelpful to Stalin left unpublished until the Russian archive was opened after 1991, when over 6,000 writings were found to have gone unpublished.

Historians disagree. Supporters see a champion of revolutionary socialism and internationalism; Richard Pipes and Robert Gellately wrote hostile biographies, and Christopher Hill sympathetic ones. Many historians call his government a police state and him a dictator, though Fischer noted that he was not the kind of dictator Stalin became, and Volkogonov wrote that he built a dictatorship of the party before Stalin's of one man. Western historians long saw Stalinism as a continuation of Leninism until revisionists such as Moshe Lewin broke the consensus in the late 1960s. Marxist writers such as Hill and John Rees reject the view that Lenin's government was a dictatorship, and Ryan argues that for Lenin revolutionary violence was a means to a world without violence. In 2024 a Levada poll found 67% of Russians believed he played a positive role in the country's history.

summary: Vladimir Lenin (1870–1924) led the Bolsheviks to power in Russia in October 1917 and headed the Soviet government until his death. His government won the civil war and founded the Soviet Union, but ruled through the Cheka and the Red Terror. Historians and political camps still disagree about him.
references: Louis Fischer, The Life of Lenin (Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1964)
Catherine Merridale, Lenin on the Train (Penguin, 2017)
Moshe Lewin, Lenin's Last Struggle (Faber & Faber, 1969)
Richard Pipes, The Unknown Lenin: From the Secret Archive (Yale University Press, 1996)

The article gives 'between 1917 and 1922 / 1923' for the Civil War in different places; not used as a date. Its infobox-style claim that the 1922 Soviet Union reunited five nations by force is in the lead; I gave it only through the article's body.
